papers.title: Waveform morphology links local circuit kinetics to cortical interactions
papers.abstract: How does local cortical physiology shape interactions between brain regions? We combined neural mass modelling with human and macaque intracranial recordings to examine how synaptic kinetics link oscillatory waveform morphology to cortical interactions. In a modified excitatory-inhibitory Wilson-Cowan model, synaptic rise and decay kinetics shaped waveform geometry and phase-dependent responsiveness. Local kinetics and coupling symmetry jointly influenced interaction measures and temporal irreversibility, while phase-locked perturbations altered imaginary coherency and bivariate irreversibility even when the coupling strengths remained fixed. In stereo-EEG from 23 patients, waveform asymmetry was most strongly associated with local irreversibility, whereas mean instantaneous alpha frequency showed stronger associations with interregional measures. Subdural macaque electrocorticography reproduced the frequency associations but not the local waveform association. Together, these findings show that waveform shape carries information about local neuronal dynamics, provide a mechanistic framework for interpreting cortical interactions, and motivate testing waveform morphology as a guide to stimulation timing.

papers.title: Slow-Wave Enhancement Reduces Axonal Injury in Murine Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability as well as impaired cognition and sleep-wake abnormalities. The pathological hallmark of TBI is disturbed axonal transport and accumulation of proteins, leading to diffuse axonal injury (DAI). Recent studies suggest a role for slow-wave sleep (SWS) in the clearance of harmful extracellular proteins and functional recovery. Our group previously found that increasing SWS after TBI in rats improved cognition and decreased accumulation of injury-related histological markers in cortex and hippocampus, indicating a neuroprotective role of SWS. Though growing evidence suggests that sleep can improve the outcome of TBI, prior mouse models of TBI were incompatible with sleep recordings. In the current study, we modified the classical weight-drop mouse model to be compatible with a headset for recording electroencephalogram (EEG) and electromyogram, and to replicate effects of SWS modulation on TBI outcome measures. The resulting mild TBI mouse model shows cognitive impairment, EEG abnormalities, and DAI. Such DAI was reduced following treatment with sodium oxybate during the first 3 days after trauma, concomitant with increased slow-wave activity. Chemogenetic modulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, on the other hand, did not reduce slow-wave activity. Overall, in the present study, we characterized an adapted weight-drop mouse TBI model for studying the relationship between sleep and TBI and provided additional evidence on involvement of sleep in neuronal recovery.

papers.title: EEG-Derived Proxies of Cortical Excitability in Epilepsy: Group Discrimination, Temporal Stability and Medication Sensitivity
papers.abstract: Objective To identify EEG-derived markers of cortical excitability that best distinguish people with epilepsy from healthy controls while maintaining stability across repeated recordings, and to assess the influence of antiseizure medication (ASM) burden on these measures. Methods Scalp EEG recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Epilepsy Corpus were analyzed, including 1,404 recordings from 96 individuals with neurologist-confirmed epilepsy and 85 healthy controls across multiple sessions. Eight global EEG measures were evaluated: aperiodic exponent and offset, sample entropy, detrended fluctuation analysis exponent and derived index, spatial gamma-band phase consistency, and absolute and relative alpha power. Primary group inference used linear mixed-effects models to account for repeated recordings and sessions within participants. Secondary analyses examined group differences in measures temporal stability and cross-metric correlation. We examined only in epilepsy group associations between EEG-derived metrics and ASMs count, and their impact on cross-metric correlations. Results In the mixed-effects models, aperiodic offset and exponent were the only measures with FDR-robust group effects. Aperiodic offset showed higher consistency in epilepsy than in healthy controls (standardized epilepsy-minus-healthy beta = 0.52, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.78, FDR-adjusted p = 0.001). Across sessions, consistency was higher in epilepsy for aperiodic offset exponent (beta = 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.54, FDR-adjusted p = 0.018). Cross-metric correlation patterns were largely preserved between groups. Medication associations were examined separately within the epilepsy group. Higher ASM burden was associated with higher alpha relative power. Significance Among eight candidate EEG measures aperiodic offset and exponent differed between groups (epilepsy vs. healthy controls), and both were more reproducible across sessions in epilepsy. Relative alpha power tracked within-person antiseizure medication burden, suggesting that disease-related and treatment-related EEG markers may be complementary. These findings, obtained from routine clinical EEG in an open dataset, suggest aperiodic spectral parameters as candidates for prospective validation as biomarkers.

Both aperiodic measures were more reproducible across sessions in epilepsy, and higher antiseizure medication burden was associated with higher relative alpha power.

papers.title: Image-grounded encoding models reveal distinct temporal profiles of naturalistic object and scene processing in the human brain
papers.abstract: In real-world vision, the human brain needs to process large amounts of information to effectively interact with its environment. It is well established that our visual system has specialized regions to process information efficiently, such as scene-, face-, and object-selective areas, which can be uncovered using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). However, functional localizers typically use artificially separated stimuli (e.g. scene backgrounds vs. object cutouts), and fMRI signals are insensitive to potential temporal processing differences. Here, we identify temporal signatures of object and scene processing in real-world visual environments by building image-grounded brain-predictive encoding models of human electroencephalography (EEG) responses. In a large set of high-resolution natural images, we first separate object-bound from scene-bound features on a per-image basis, and then used these features to train separate deep neural network-based encoding models to predict EEG responses to the full, intact images. We find that encoding models trained on object-bound features consistently exhibit a delayed temporal encoding profile compared to models trained on scene-bound features. Control analyses confirm the robustness of this delayed object encoding, showing that a consistent separation of objects from scene parts is needed to achieve a temporal distinction. Using these distinct encoding profiles as processing templates, we reveal the typicality of individual image elements as objects or part of the scene. These findings demonstrate that object and scene processing in the human brain unfold differentially over time and indicate that image-grounded encoding models are helpful tools for isolating components of naturalistic visual perception.

papers.title: Spectral power and functional connectivity alterations in multiple system atrophy revealed by resting-state EEG.
papers.abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is an aggressive α-synucleinopathy characterized by motor and autonomic dysfunction. Elucidating neurophysiological patterns can provide crucial insights into the underlying neural mechanisms. Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and fMRI data were collected from 69 healthy controls and 123 MSA patients, comprising a discovery cohort (n = 97) and an independent validation cohort (n = 26). MSA patients showed reduced delta power in the cerebellar, frontoparietal, visual I, and limbic networks, with widespread increases in theta and high gamma power. Amplitude-based connectivity decreased across the alpha, beta, and gamma bands in subcortical, cerebellar, default mode, motor, and visual I networks, with increased theta-band synchrony involving motor, visual II, and frontoparietal networks. These EEG abnormalities were corroborated by fMRI connectivity, highlighting cross-modal consistency. Canonical correlation analysis revealed associations between EEG features and motor/non-motor symptom severity. Interpretable stacking models accurately classified MSA-C and MSA-P subtypes and predicted UMSARS progression in longitudinal follow-up. These findings identified aberrant neural activity and network dysfunction in MSA, highlighting EEG as a promising biomarker for disease monitoring.

ai.reason: Uses spectral power and connectivity with interpretable stacking models, but is clinical disease-classification rather than a transferable methodology or animal sleep application.

EEG features correlated with motor/non-motor symptom severity, and interpretable stacking models classified MSA-C versus MSA-P subtypes and predicted UMSARS progression.

papers.title: Wearable sensing technologies and machine learning for fatigue assessment in sport horses.
papers.abstract: Fatigue in sport horses is a multifactorial phenomenon that critically affects performance, injury risk, and welfare, yet its real-time, field-based assessment remains an unmet challenge. To synthesise evidence on the use of wearable sensors and machine learning for fatigue-related monitoring in sport horses and to identify priorities for future fatigue assessment. Scoping review. This scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Publications from 2015 to 2026 were identified through Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect. Evidence from 102 publications was synthesised across five sensing modalities-heart rate (HR)/heart rate variability (HRV), thermometry, inertial measurement units (IMUs), surface electromyography (sEMG), and GPS-alongside machine learning applications for feature extraction, state classification, and risk modelling. Our synthesis reveals a fundamental disconnect: while each technology captures distinct physiological or biomechanical correlates of load, including autonomic response, thermoregulatory strain, gait stability, neuromuscular activation, and external workload, none provides a standalone signature of fatigue. Only a minority of studies used fatigue as a direct modelling label, with most relying on proxy outcomes such as asymmetry or performance decrement. The included literature was heterogeneous in sensor modalities, study designs, outcome measures, and application contexts. In addition, the limited use of directly defined fatigue outcomes restricted comparison across studies and constrained conclusions regarding fatigue-specific monitoring. The path forward lies not in developing yet another single-sensor solution, but in establishing a multidimensional, context-aware framework that integrates complementary data streams, individualised baselines, and interpretable models. Future research should prioritise: (1) operationalised fatigue definitions; (2) longitudinal, within-horse monitoring designs; (3) robust multimodal fusion architectures; (4) rigorous external validation across equestrian disciplines; and (5) explainable artificial intelligence to bridge the gap between algorithmic output and actionable training decisions.

papers.title: Development and EEG Assessment of a Virtual Reality Replica of a Prior Real Multisensory Environment Intervention.
papers.abstract: Multisensory environments (MSEs) are valuable therapeutic spaces for relaxation and stress relief, yet high costs and physical infrastructure limit accessibility. Immersive virtual reality MSEs (V-MSEs) offer a low-cost and scalable alternative to real MSEs (R-MSEs), but evidence is scarce. The aim of this study is an exploratory characterization of the electroencephalography (EEG) response to a V-MSE replica of a previous R-MSE intervention, using the original R-MSE data as a qualitative reference. After developing a V-MSE mirroring the original environment, 31 healthy participants underwent an adapted version of the protocol, and spectral and nonlinear features were computed from EEG recordings pre- and post-intervention. Analyses were performed within each environment, and comparisons between them remained qualitative. The alpha/beta ratio, negatively correlated with stress, was the only feature significantly increased in both conditions. In the V-MSE, frontal theta and the theta/beta ratio also increased significantly, whereas relative gamma power and Lempel-Ziv complexity decreased. Only in R-MSE, parieto-occipital alpha power rose significantly, whereas frontal delta power decreased. No feature changed significantly in opposite directions between settings. Evidence remains insufficient to establish V-MSEs as an alternative to R-MSEs, but this first EEG characterization of a V-MSE is encouraging enough to justify broader studies.

papers.title: Direction-specific effects of biphasic transcranial magnetic stimulation on cortical and cortico-spinal excitability.
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a well-established tool for inducing cortical excitation. However, the relevance of current direction on elicited effects is still incompletely understood. Combining TMS with electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) enables non-invasive analysis of evoked potentials both on cortical and peripheral level. In 23 healthy subjects, EEG and EMG responses to biphasic single pulses applied over the left motor cortex with anterior-posterior to posterior-anterior (AP-PA) or PA-AP current direction and 110% resting motor threshold (RMT) intensity were recorded and contrasted between the alternating phases. A cobot-assisted neuronavigation ensured stable coil-placement during the procedure. RMT was lower and EMG latency was shorter for AP-PA currents compared to PA-AP currents, whereas the EMG amplitude did not differ. For EEG responses, local and global evoked activity was higher for mid-components with PA-AP currents. P60 occurred earlier with PA-AP currents and N100 amplitude was higher in amplitude with AP-PA currents. The trial-wise MEP amplitude correlated significantly with P30 in the AP-PA and for both current directions with the N100 amplitude. Our results highlight the directional sensitivity of M1 and the importance of further exploring the role of current direction in TMS protocols to better understand the cortical processes underlying cortico-cortical and cortico-spinal responses.

ai.reason: Combined EEG/EMG evoked-potential analysis is adjacent signal-processing content, but TMS-stimulation specific and not sleep/state oriented.
ai.summary: Combined TMS with EEG and EMG in 23 healthy subjects to contrast biphasic pulses over left motor cortex applied in AP-PA versus PA-AP current directions at 110% resting motor threshold. AP-PA currents produced lower RMT and shorter EMG latency with higher N100 amplitudes, whereas PA-AP currents yielded higher mid-component cortical evoked activity and earlier P60, demonstrating direction-specific cortical and cortico-spinal effects.

papers.title: Invasive monitoring and mapping in epilepsy surgery: Acute and chronic intracranial recording from surface to depth.
papers.abstract: Invasive intracranial recording remains central to the surgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy when noninvasive data are insufficient to define the epileptogenic zone or its relationship to eloquent cortex. This review, part of an International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) Surgical Therapies Commission education series aligned with the epilepsy surgery curriculum, reviews invasive monitoring and mapping for the practicing and trainee epilepsy surgeon. Consistent with the competency-based ILAE epilepsy surgery curriculum, in which the surgeon is expected to understand and actively contribute to electrode selection, safe implantation, and the interpretation of invasive recordings within the multidisciplinary team, we give particular emphasis to the surgical execution of these methods alongside their electrophysiological rationale. We outline the historical development of the field from intraoperative electrocorticography and subdural recording to stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG), describe acute and chronic recording strategies using both surface and depth approaches, including the operative techniques of implantation and post-implantation electrode localization, and summarize the techniques of functional mapping. We compare subdural and stereotactic methods with respect to coverage, mapping capability, diagnostic yield, seizure outcome, and morbidity, and we review the complication profiles of each. Finally, we discuss future directions, including high-density and chronically implantable probes that combine macro-contacts with microelectrode recording throughout the electrode shaft. We emphasize that the choice of method should follow a clearly stated anatomo-electro-clinical hypothesis, balancing the completeness of sampling against procedural risk.
authors: Tatiana V H F de Oliveira

papers.title: Syndrome-oriented CNS infectious complications after hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and CAR T-cell therapy, part 1-viral encephalitis, meningitis, and myelitis: recommendations from the Practice Harmonization & Guidelines Committee of the EBMT.
papers.abstract: Viral encephalitis, meningitis, and myelitis are rare but life-threatening complications after autologous or allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HSCT) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, associated with 30-60% mortality and frequent neurological sequelae. The absence of harmonised definitions and diagnostic criteria contributes to delayed diagnosis, underreporting, and substantial heterogeneity across centres. This EBMT Practice Harmonization and Guidelines Committee expert consensus provides practical recommendations for the definition, diagnosis, treatment, response assessment, and prevention of viral encephalitis/meningitis and viral myelitis, developed through systematic literature review and multidisciplinary expert consensus following EBMT methodology. We propose standardised diagnostic categories for proven and probable viral encephalitis/meningitis and myelitis, alongside a unified diagnostic algorithm integrating clinical assessment, neuroimaging, electroencephalography, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and targeted virological testing. We highlight key neurotropic viruses for inclusion in initial cerebrospinal fluid multiplex PCR panels, including human herpesvirus 6, herpes simplex virus 1/2, varicella zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, adenovirus, polyomaviruses BK/JC, and selected community-acquired respiratory viruses, such as EV71, and recommend prompt, risk-based empirical antiviral therapy in suspected cases. These recommendations aim to standardise clinical practice, facilitate multicenter research, and improve outcomes. However, many rely on limited observational evidence or expert opinion, underscoring the need for prospective studies.

papers.title: From Synapses to Circuits: A Systematic Review of How Developmental Ethanol Exposure Alters Excitation-Inhibition Balance.
papers.abstract: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is a prevalent cause of neurodevelopmental impairment associated with lifelong cognitive and behavioral deficits. These difficulties may arise partly because developmental ethanol exposure disrupts the balance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) signaling. Acute ethanol exposure can suppress excitation through NMDA receptors and enhance inhibition through GABA_A receptors, thereby reducing neural activity. However, its longer-term effects on synaptic communication in the developing brain remain unclear. We systematically reviewed studies published from 2000 through December 2025 that used whole-cell electrophysiology to measure excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs and IPSCs) following developmental alcohol exposure. The review was limited to rat and mouse studies because these species are the principal experimental models of developmental ethanol exposure and allow comparisons across established developmental stages. Whole-cell studies were selected because they provide direct, cell-resolved measurements of spontaneous and miniature postsynaptic currents; field recordings, EEG, and other network-level approaches were outside the predefined scope. Twenty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. Sixteen examined inhibitory currents, 20 examined excitatory currents, and nine assessed E/I balance. Most studies reported increased frequencies of miniature or spontaneous IPSCs following developmental ethanol exposure. In contrast, EPSC frequency varied by brain region and developmental time point, with both increases and decreases reported. No consistent directional shift emerged among studies assessing E/I balance. Developmental ethanol exposure therefore appears to alter inhibitory synaptic transmission more consistently than excitatory transmission, while its overall effects on E/I balance are heterogeneous and circuit-dependent. These findings highlight the need for systematic, region-specific, and developmentally targeted studies to clarify how altered synaptic signaling contributes to cognitive and behavioral dysfunction in FASD.

ai.reason: Patch-clamp synaptic physiology review; explicitly excludes EEG/network-level approaches, so only tangential relevance.
ai.summary: A systematic review of 25 whole-cell electrophysiology studies (2000–2025) in rat and mouse models examining how developmental ethanol exposure alters excitatory/inhibitory balance. Most studies reported increased frequencies of miniature or spontaneous IPSCs, whereas EPSC frequency varied by brain region and developmental time point, and no consistent directional shift in E/I balance emerged, indicating more consistent inhibitory effects and circuit-dependent heterogeneity.

papers.title: Neurophysiological changes following intensive Naikan therapy in a patient with recurrent depressive episodes later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder: A case report.
papers.abstract: Intensive Naikan therapy is a structured Japanese psychotherapy involving systematic reflection on interpersonal relationships; however, its neurophysiological correlates remain unclear. We herein report changes in resting-state electroencephalography (EEG), the P300 event-related potential, and standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA)-estimated source activity after intensive Naikan therapy. A 29-year-old man with recurrent depressive episodes and anxiety about family relationships and future employment underwent 7 days of inpatient intensive Naikan therapy. He was later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder after a hypomanic episode during the follow-up. Assessments were performed before and after the intervention. Anxiety decreased on State-Trait Anxiety Inventory state and trait scores (42 to 20 and 30 to 20, respectively), and depressive symptoms remained minimal on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and Beck Depression Inventory (4 to 3 and 0 to 0, respectively). Psychological measures suggested reduced self- and other-blame and greater acceptance of family members. Resting-state EEG showed a negligible change in peak alpha-band global field power, whereas peak beta-band global field power decreased from 5.13 × 103 to 2.84 × 103 µV2/Hz. During the auditory oddball task, P300 amplitude at Pz increased from 5.5 to 7.3 µV. sLORETA images were evaluated descriptively, without statistical comparisons or uncertainty estimations. Intensive Naikan therapy was temporally associated with reduced resting-state beta activity and an increased P300 amplitude. These observations from a single uncontrolled case with multiple assessments are hypothesis-generating and do not establish treatment efficacy, causality, or a treatment mechanism.

The single uncontrolled case is hypothesis-generating and does not establish efficacy or mechanism.

papers.title: Circadian rhythm in the atrioventricular node - in electrophysiology, contractility, metabolism, intracellular signalling and extracellular matrix
papers.abstract: The atrioventricular (AV) node shows a circadian rhythm-during sleep the PR interval is longer (because conduction velocity is decreased) and AV block is more common. We show the rhythm is similar in mouse and human, and using mice we have investigated the cause. There was still a rhythm in Kcnj5 knockout mice ruling out a major role of vagal tone (the vagus regulates the node via Kcnj5). Instead, we show the presence of a functioning circadian clock in the node (e.g. by detection of rhythmic clock transcripts). There was ~43-52% reduction in the rhythm of the PR interval on inhibition of the clock in a Bmal1 knockout mouse. There was a significant rhythm in >300 intracellular signalling molecules presumably driven by the clock and perhaps extrinsic signals. Downstream of the clock and signalling molecules, there was a rhythm in many transcripts and proteins (of 4,186 proteins, ~15% had a rhythm), responsible for example for contractile machinery, metabolism, extracellular matrix, and importantly ion channels. Ultimately, the PR interval is determined by ion channels, and there were rhythms in ion channels and ionic currents. A key determinant of conduction velocity is the upstroke velocity of the Ca2+-dependent nodal action potential and this was significantly reduced during sleep, this can be explained by reduced expression of Ca2+ channel subunits and a smaller L-type Ca2+ current at this time and this was confirmed by biophysically-detailed computer modelling. In conclusion, there is day-night molecular remodelling of the AV node and this is largely responsible for the circadian rhythm in the PR interval.

ai.reason: Cardiac circadian ion-channel physiology; only a keyword collision on 'sleep' and 'electrophysiology', not neural time-series analysis.
ai.summary: Using mouse and human data, this study shows a circadian rhythm in the atrioventricular node that prolongs PR interval during sleep and is largely independent of vagal tone, driven instead by a local circadian clock; Bmal1 knockout reduced the PR rhythm by ~43-52%. Molecular remodeling includes rhythms in >300 signaling molecules and ~15% of 4,186 proteins, including ion channels, with reduced L-type Ca2+ current and upstroke velocity during sleep confirmed by computer modeling.

papers.title: Postoperative hemispheric hyperperfusion and status epilepticus after chronic subdural hematoma evacuation: a case report.
papers.abstract: Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome (CHS) is rarely reported after chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) evacuation. We describe a 40-year-old man who developed right hemispheric swelling, neurological deterioration, generalized seizures, and ipsilateral hyperperfusion on computed tomography perfusion after burr-hole drainage of a right CSDH. The overall clinical and radiological course was most consistent with probable CHS complicated by refractory status epilepticus, although seizure-related ictal or postictal hyperperfusion could not be fully excluded. He required strict blood pressure control, antiseizure therapy, deep intravenous anesthesia, and continuous electroencephalographic monitoring. Serial perfusion imaging showed gradual resolution of the hyperperfusion. He was discharged without neurological deficits and had returned to work with a modified Rankin Scale score of 0 by postoperative day 45. At 1 year, he remained seizure-free after withdrawal of all antiseizure medications, and an outside-hospital 24-hour ambulatory electroencephalography report showed no epileptiform abnormalities.

ai.reason: Clinical case report with continuous EEG monitoring; negligible methodological or animal-sleep relevance.
ai.summary: This case report describes a 40-year-old man who developed right hemispheric hyperperfusion, neurological deterioration, generalized seizures, and refractory status epilepticus after burr-hole drainage of a chronic subdural hematoma, most consistent with probable cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome. He was managed with strict blood pressure control, antiseizure therapy, deep intravenous anesthesia, and continuous EEG, with gradual resolution and no neurological deficits at discharge and seizure freedom at 1 year.

papers.title: Intrinsic Sweetness and Sweetness-Enhancing Property of β-Damascone.
papers.abstract: β-Damascone is a naturally occurring aroma compound with pronounced fruity-floral and "sweet-smelling" notes. Although well characterized olfactorily, its gustatory role and sweetness-enhancing property remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the intrinsic sweetness of β-damascone and its ability to enhance sucrose-induced sweetness using an integrative approach combining sensory evaluation, electroencephalography (EEG), molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. Sensory evaluation showed that β-damascone alone elicited negligible sweetness, but significantly amplified and prolonged sucrose-induced sweetness. EEG measurements further revealed strengthened cortical responses during co-stimulation with sucrose. Using a cryo-EM-derived full-length TAS1R2-TAS1R3-membrane model, molecular simulations demonstrated that β-damascone binds to a peripheral region of LB1-LB2 cleft in TAS1R2 VFD, stabilizing its closed conformation. β-Damascone also facilitated conformational rearrangements associated with receptor activation, including widening of the intracellular G-protein-binding cavity. Collectively, these findings provide mechanistic evidence that β-damascone acts as a synergistic enhancer of sucrose sweetness, supporting its potential for sugar-reduction applications.

ai.reason: Gustatory/chemosensory study; EEG only as an incidental measure, keyed to food science, not neural time-series methods.
ai.summary: Combining sensory evaluation, EEG, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics with a TAS1R2-TAS1R3 model, this study found that β-damascone alone has negligible intrinsic sweetness but significantly amplifies and prolongs sucrose-induced sweetness, with strengthened cortical responses during co-stimulation. Simulations indicate β-damascone binds a peripheral region of the TAS1R2 VFD LB1-LB2 cleft, stabilizing a closed conformation and facilitating activation-associated rearrangements, supporting its potential for sugar reduction.

papers.title: Diet and Sex Influence Central Amygdala Neuroimmune Regulation of Binge Behaviors.
papers.abstract: Central amygdala (CeA) neuroimmune signaling is thought to play a critical role in binge behavior toward ethanol (EtOH) and high-fat diet (HFD), but the specific mechanisms by which CeA neuroimmune activity regulates binge intake, and how this system may be impacted by diet and sex, remain unclear. To test this, we assessed intermittent HFD/limited-access EtOH (iHFD + EtOH) intake with chemogenetic Gi-DREADD modulation of CeA astrocytes timed either immediately before drinking sessions or during HFD access in male mice. We then assessed CeA astrocytic Ca2+ dynamics and whole-cell electrophysiology of CeA glutamatergic transmission. We further compared impacts of two lab maintenance "chow" diets (Teklad 8604 vs. Bio-Serv F4031) on iHFD + EtOH intake in males and females and preliminarily assessed changes to two major CeA neuroimmune signals. Gi-DREADD actuation in CeA astrocytes immediately prior to drinking sessions selectively reduced EtOH intake, suggesting CeA astrocytes provide session-proximal control over EtOH behaviors. Gi-DREADD actuation in CeA astrocytes during iHFD access periods did not reduce HFD or EtOH intake. Prior iHFD + EtOH history sensitized CeA astrocyte Ca2+ responses to EtOH and elevated baseline and EtOH-evoked glutamatergic drive. Maintenance diets differentially impacted EtOH intake and modified CeA IL-10 and IL-13 levels, dependent on diet, sex, and binge history. Together, these data indicate that CeA astrocytes exert session-proximal control over binge-like EtOH intake, and diet/EtOH history sensitizes both CeA astrocyte signaling and CeA glutamate transmission. Critically, maintenance diets and sex may interact as modulators of drinking phenotypes and CeA neuroimmune signals. These findings identify CeA astrocytes as mechanistic entry points for interventions and establish diet and sex as essential experimental variables for studies of binge alcohol and palatable food intake.

ai.reason: Rodent behavioral/neuroimmune study with whole-cell electrophysiology; not time-series or sleep-EEG methodology.
ai.summary: Used chemogenetic Gi-DREADD astrocyte modulation, Ca2+ imaging, and electrophysiology in male mice to show that central amygdala astrocytes exert session-proximal control over binge-like ethanol intake, and that intermittent high-fat diet plus ethanol history sensitizes CeA astrocyte Ca2+ responses and glutamatergic drive; maintenance diet and sex modulated ethanol intake and CeA IL-10/IL-13 levels.

papers.title: A Novel DHX9 Variant Was Identified in a Patient With Developmental Delay, Facial Dysmorphism and Seizure.
papers.abstract: The DHX9 gene encodes an RNA helicase belonging to the DExD/H-box family, which is highly expressed in the brain and nervous system. Pathogenic variants in the DHX9 gene are associated with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT). Both loss-of-function (LoF) and missense variants can cause NDD, whereas CMT is associated with specific missense variants. Patients with DHX9-related NDD typically present with intellectual disability, language and motor developmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). CMT patients primarily present with distal weakness, sensory deficits, variable muscle wasting, foot deformities and painful sensory neuropathy. Here, we report a female patient with severe DHX9-related NDD phenotypes, including global developmental delay, ASD, facial dysmorphism, epilepsy, microcephaly, abnormal brain MRI findings and clinodactyly of the fifth finger. She experienced her first febrile seizure at 1 year and 2 months of age. She developed frequent myoclonic seizures characterized by rapid nodding and upper body tremors lasting 3-10 s at the age of 3 years. Simultaneous electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed paroxysmal bursts of high- to very-high-amplitude sharp-slow waves, spike-slow waves and polyspike-wave complexes diffusely over bilateral leads. Clinical exome sequencing (CES) identified a likely de novo missense variant in the DHX9 gene in the patient (NM_001357.5, c.1540C>T, p.(His514Tyr)). Notably, this variant resides within the highly conserved DEIH motif (Motif II) of the helicase ATP-binding domain. This critical region plays an essential role in ATP hydrolysis and helicase function. Three-dimensional protein structure modelling suggested that the p.(His514Tyr) substitution may compromise local protein stability by altering hydrogen bond networks. Our study expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of DHX9 variant-associated disorders.

papers.title: Synergistic electro-mechanical stimulation promotes neural stem cell differentiation in a 3D conductive and stretchable hydrogel.
papers.abstract: The limited understanding of how to physically manipulate neural stem cell (NSC) differentiation into mature neurons and functional glial cells in a three-dimensional (3D) environment has constrained the potential of NSC-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. In this study, we develop gelatin-methacryloyl (GelMA) and polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA)-based conductive hydrogels to investigate the effects of electrical stimulation (ES) and mechanical stretching on neuronal differentiation in a 3D matrix. GelMA and PEGDA provide extracellular matrix (ECM)-like biological and physical characteristics, enabling the study of neural differentiation, development, and electrophysiology. Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) was incorporated into the GelMA/PEGDA matrix as a conductive additive to enhance hydrogel conductivity. Compared with non-conductive hydrogels, conductive hydrogels alone promoted neuronal differentiation, while conductive hydrogels combined with ES further enhanced neural differentiation, neurite extension, and neural gene expression. Mechanical stretching similarly induced neuronal differentiation and directional neurite alignment. Notably, co-stimulation with stretching and ES exerted synergistic effects, significantly promoting neurite outgrowth (2.5-fold compared to the unstimulated hydrogel control (GelMA-PEGDA)), increasing filopodia density by 15%, and enhancing neurite branching by 3%. Co-stimulation also upregulated neuronal differentiation marker expression, including for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neuron-specific class III β-tubulin (Tuj-1), and microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2), and increased the neuronal electrical activity of encapsulated cells. Overall, this study advances the understanding of directed NSC differentiation within a 3D microenvironment using defined physical cues and provides a theoretical basis for improving the effectiveness and feasibility of NSC-based therapies.

papers.title: Reducing the diagnostic odyssey in childhood-onset non-5q spinal muscular atrophy through phenotype-guided genomic evaluation.
papers.abstract: Childhood-onset non-5q spinal muscular atrophies (SMA) comprise a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of neuromuscular disorders in which molecular diagnosis may be delayed despite increasing access to next-generation and whole-exome sequencing. Although broad genomic testing has transformed diagnostic practice, its interpretation remains highly dependent on detailed clinical characterization. We emphasize the value of phenotype-guided genomic evaluation in children with suspected non-5q SMA. Age at onset, distribution of weakness, tendon reflexes, respiratory and skeletal involvement, creatine kinase levels, electrophysiological findings, family history, and targeted neuroimaging may reveal recognizable genotype-associated patterns that help prioritize candidate genes and facilitate variant interpretation. A recently reported pediatric case series illustrates characteristic associations including scapuloperoneal weakness with TRPV4 variants, congenital hypotonia and arthrogryposis with ASCC1-related disease, lower-extremity-predominant weakness with BICD2, pontocerebellar hypoplasia with VRK1, and bilateral thalamic abnormalities with HEXB variants. Rather than replacing genomic technologies, comprehensive phenotyping provides the clinical framework required to maximize their diagnostic yield. Following exclusion of SMN1-related disease, integrating clinical examination, electrophysiology, neuroimaging, and broad genomic sequencing may help reduce the diagnostic odyssey in childhood-onset non-5q SMA.

papers.title: Oral glycoside supplement (triterpenoid saponins) for early and intermediate stage age-related macular degeneration (SAMADI trial): study protocol for a double masked randomised placebo-controlled feasibility trial.
papers.abstract: The primary aim of the SAMADI [SAponins for MAcular DIsease] trial is to establish whether treatment of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with oral saponin supplements is feasible and acceptable to participants. AMD is a progressive disease, which results in the death and dysfunction of cells in the outer retina. One potential contributor to AMD progression is the reduced permeability of Bruch's membrane underlying the retina. Saponins have a structure enabling them to assist dispersal of lipid deposits in Bruch's membrane, providing a rationale for the proposed intervention in AMD. Secondary aims are to provide an estimate of the variability of a proposed future primary outcome, and to provide estimates of treatment effects of clinical outcomes. SAMADI is a double masked randomised feasibility trial, which will recruit 60 participants with early or intermediate AMD in at least one eye. Participants will be randomly assigned into one of two groups, one receiving the oral saponin tablets and the other placebo tablets (indistinguishable in appearance), both to be taken daily for 4 months. Participants and research optometrists will be masked to the allocation. Clinical tests will be repeated at baseline, 4 months and 12 months. The primary outcome measures relate to feasibility of the following aspects of the intervention and study design: (1) recruitment and retention over 4 and 12 months; (2) adherence to treatment and acceptability of intervention; (3) the eligibility assessment process; (4) collecting the outcome data. The rate of serious adverse events will be an additional primary outcome measure. Secondary outcomes include dark adaptation metrics, best corrected visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, fundus imaging, low luminance questionnaire, standard electroretinograms according to International Society for Clinical Electrophysiology of Vision standard protocols, and imaging retinal densitometry (at one site only). The data will be used to determine the feasibility of the trial design, how well participants complied with taking the tablets, and the potential effectiveness of the treatment. If feasible, this information will be used to inform a larger trial, which will definitively assess how effective the treatment is in participants with AMD. The trial is registered with EudraCT and ISRCTN registries. EudraCT ref: 2021-003045-38; Date of registration: 24/05/2021. ISRCTN ref: ISRCTN82949875; Date of registration: July 21, 2021. URL: https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN82949875 . Version and date: This report is based on Protocol V3, January 2024.
